(Click here to hear the statement in full, as posted by ABC News .) Four people died in the Thursday shooting at Silver Rail Elementary School: a 5-year-old kindergartner, Rhoam Summer ; two boys, ages 8 and 11, who have not been publicly named; and Lambert. The suspect in the shooting, 16-year-old Griffin John II, is a former Silver Rail student; John was shot and killed by a parent . Silver Rail was Lambert’s first teaching job, the family said in its statement. “She loved Silver Rail,” the family said. “This was her dream job.” Lambert joined Bend schools this fall as a special education teacher. “Megan was a bright light for her students, family, and our community,” school officials said in a message to the Silver Rail community . “She will be missed beyond words can express.”

items.summary: A 46-year-old graduate student, a 12-year-old homeschooler and an 18-year-old college freshman gathered with others on a sunny Tuesday afternoon at Moscow High to kick off the last week of an archeological dig. items.body: A 46-year-old graduate student, a 12-year-old homeschooler and an 18-year-old college freshman gathered with others on a sunny Tuesday afternoon at Moscow High to kick off the last week of an archeological dig. The dig is part of a continuing push by the university’s anthropology department to help Idahoans connect to their own history through archeology — and connect with each other through a shared interest. This fall marks the third time the group has dug at the high school, built in the 1930s. Organizers say it was also the most productive, with students discovering a corner of the original 1890 school that was demolished years ago to make way for the current high school. Students also dug in what was once an alley behind area homes, uncovering artifacts of daily life, like buttons, a doll face and remnants of dishes. Graduate students recently started a project underneath Moscow’s public library, where they discovered hundreds of intact literary artifacts, like bookbinding supplies, ink pads and lightbulbs. The program provides students with real-world experience that is typically offered through a field school, where they often pay to travel to a remote location to complete a dig during a school break. Other community members are also welcome to participate. “It gives them more than just the skills training — it gives them the why,” said Katrina Eichner, associate professor of anthropology. “It’s not just fun for us to play in the dirt. This is important to people because it’s their history.” University of Idaho anthropology professors Katrina Eichner and Renae Campbell help students at an archaeological dig at Moscow High. About a third of University of Idaho attendees are first-generation college students. They are often from Idaho or the region, and it can be intimidating to consider spending between $3,000 to $10,000 to fly abroad or to another state for a six-to-eight-week fieldwork course. “A lot of people pay for their projects through tuition,” Eichner noted. (Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) In the race for Idaho’s top election official, two familiar names are headed to the ballot. Democratic challenger Shawn Keenan is again challenging Republican incumbent Secretary of State Phil McGrane , who widely defeated Keenan in the 2022 election. Keenan, a mortgage broker and loan officer who lives in Coeur d’Alene, says he’s running again to avoid and combat election misinformation. McGrane, a seasoned Idaho election official seeking a second term, says he’s running on a track record of keeping elections secure and improving access to election information. The two will be on the ballot in the Nov. 3 general election. The secretary of state is a statewide office that oversees elections in the state, manages campaign finance compliance and transparency, and maintains records on businesses. The secretary of state also serves on the Land Board, which manages the state’s endowment lands. The secretary of state serves a four-year term and earns an annual salary of $128,690. In a Republican-controlled state, Keenan’s election bid faces tough odds. Voters in the state last elected a Democrat to statewide office in 2002, for the superintendent of public instruction. The state last had a Democratic secretary of state decades earlier. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE Who is Shawn Keenan, the Democratic candidate for secretary of state? Idaho Democratic candidate for secretary of state, Shawn Keenan. (Photo courtesy of Shawn Keenan) Keenan, 49, has not worked in election administration but said he has been involved in politics from a young age and has worked on several Democratic campaigns in North Idaho. His parents moved to Idaho with him when he was 1 years old, he said. Keenan runs a nonprofit, called the North Idaho Kindness Project, that focuses on fostering acts of kindness — like love letters around Valentine’s Day and kindness tokens, which his group encourages people to hand out to people they see doing random acts of kindness. He said his initial bid for secretary of state four years ago came out of fear of growing distrust in election results — including among some of the then-Republican candidates for secretary of state. Years later, Keenan is still campaigning on that. “When people start crafting these stories about elections not being secure or safe in Idaho, I wanted to be a voice for the truth: that they are indeed safe and secure and have been and always will be,” he said. Keenan praised McGrane, the incumbent, for his “due diligence.” And he said he and McGrane are on the same page on at least one policy priority: Establishing a state-issued voter guide, like other Western states have, that mails information on candidates and more directly to voters. As a Democrat in a reliably red state, he said he acknowledged that his odds of getting elected are tough — unless he puts in years of doorknocking. He said his campaign has largely focused on digital outreach to voters, compared to travel across the state. With less than three weeks until the election, Keenan’s campaign has not raised any money, according to the state’s campaign finance database . Educational exhibits are placed along the trail to provide information. (Photo courtesy of the National Park Service) The Friends of Minidoka nonprofit will host its 2026 symposium, which will feature a film screening, legal discussion and lecture, “to consider the enduring importance of due process, equal protection, and civic engagement in protecting our civil liberties and strengthening democracy,” according to a press release from the organization. The 2026 Civil Liberties Symposium, titled Law, Civil Liberties, and the Continuing Pursuit of Justice: From Wayne Collins to Today, will examine how “the unjust incarceration of Japanese Americans during World War II continues to inform contemporary debates surrounding immigration, detention, national security, and constitutional rights,” the press release said. In 1942, the Minidoka War Relocation Center was constructed in Jerome County at Hunt, Idaho. Locally, it was known as “Hunt Camp.” While in operation, the site was the seventh largest city in Idaho, incarcerating nearly 9,400 people at its peak population. (Photo courtesy of the National Archives and Records Administration) The series begins Thursday with a screening of “Wayne Collins: One Fighting Irishman,” a 30-minute documentary about the San Francisco attorney who spent more than two decades defending Japanese Americans who renounced their U.S. citizenship under duress while imprisoned at the Tule Lake Segregation Center during World War II. The screening will be followed by a discussion with Emily Croston, staff attorney with the ACLU of Idaho, and Wendy Olson, former U.S. attorney for the District of Idaho and chairwoman of the Idaho State Bar’s Diversity Section. On Nov. 5, the group will host its 2026 distinguished lecture: “Mass Deportation, Detention, and ICE: How We Got Here and What We Can Do,” presented by Kari Hong, the director of the Immigration Law Clinic at the University of Idaho College of Law. Drawing on her experience as an immigration attorney, public interest lawyer, and legal scholar, Hong will examine the history and present-day realities of immigration enforcement and detention, along with opportunities to protect the rights of affected individuals. The lecture will be followed by a moderated Q&A session with the audience. The symposium concludes Dec. 8 with an online presentation of Hong’s distinguished lecture, offering another opportunity for community members to participate and engage with these issues. “History reminds us that civil liberties can be threatened when fear and claims of national security are used to justify the erosion of constitutional protections,” said Robyn Achilles, executive director of Friends of Minidoka. “By bringing historical perspectives into conversation with today’s legal challenges, the Civil Liberties Symposium creates opportunities for our community to learn, ask difficult questions, and consider our shared responsibility to uphold justice.” All events are free and open to the public, with registration required. items.body: An orange "detour ahead" sign alerts motorists of a new route around new housing construction in Boise in summer 2026. (Photo by Abigail Gerstein/Idaho Capital Sun) Idaho’s newly approved Opportunity Zones could help bring more housing, businesses and jobs to communities across the state. The attraction for investors is the potential tax savings. This month, Idaho Commerce announced that the U.S. Treasury approved 25 zones, including areas in Boise, Coeur d’Alene and Post Falls. The new Opportunity Zone designations take effect Jan. 1. An Opportunity Zone is a designated area where the federal government offers tax benefits to encourage private investment. The idea is straightforward: give investors a financial reason to put money into communities that could benefit from more economic activity. In Boise, the five areas identified by the city are Downtown, Shoreline, University District, South Boise Village and West Boise . These are general descriptions of the selected areas. The actual boundaries determine whether a particular property is included. In North Idaho, the officially designated list includes parts of Coeur d’Alene and Post Falls, as well as areas around Blanchard and Kellogg, Smelterville and Wardner. Other designated communities include Caldwell, Garden City, Nampa, Pocatello and Twin Falls. The state’s announcement provides the complete list and a link to look up the boundaries . The program connects investors with projects that need money. An investor who sells stock, real estate or a business at a profit may face a tax bill on that gain. By investing an eligible gain through a special investment vehicle called a Qualified Opportunity Fund, the investor may receive tax benefits. The fund puts that money into qualifying property or businesses within a zone. The IRS explains the basic structure here . Imagine a business owner who sells a company and wants to invest some of the profit. Across town, a developer wants to turn an underused property into apartments with shops on the ground floor. If the project is in an Opportunity Zone and meets the program’s requirements, an Opportunity Fund could connect that investor’s money with the development. The investor receives an ownership interest, and the project receives money to help move forward. Under the new rules beginning in 2027, a qualifying investor generally can delay tax on the invested gain for five years and reduce the amount of that gain subject to tax. Holding the investment for at least 10 years may also allow the investor to avoid federal tax on qualifying growth in the investment’s value. Coeur d’Alene also offers a potential partnership story. Idaho Capital Sun reported that Kootenai County and the Coeur d’Alene Tribe both sought designation for the local tract. The application summary identified vacant tribal land as an opportunity for investment involving the Tribe, local governments, and private developers. That possibility deserves attention, although the designation itself does not establish a finalized development partnership. For investors, those benefits can make a long-term investment more attractive. For developers and business owners, the program can help attract money from people willing to wait for a project to mature. That could support a new apartment building, the redevelopment of an older commercial property, or the expansion of a qualifying business. Residents may benefit from additional homes, employment, and services. Those outcomes are possibilities, not promises. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE

items.body: Work continues on the new QTS data center in Eagle Mountain, Utah, on April 17, 2026. Today’s data center buildout has become the largest industrial boom since the railroad era of the 19th century, with $10 trillion in investment and almost twice the economic impact. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch) The sheer size of investment in data centers is drawing concern as it surpasses all other historical booms and crowds out other more job-creating ventures. Until now, no industry had driven the U.S. economy with such force since the railroad expansion of the late 1800s, when titans battled one another to lay the transcontinental tracks that would connect America from coast to coast. Railroads in the 19 th century consumed about $173 billion in today’s dollars and created more than 2% of the nation’s annual economic output (GDP) over 20 years. Today’s data center buildout will dwarf that amount, with $10 trillion in investment, and now have almost twice the economic impact — nearly 4% of GDP. That’s according to a report created by a Columbia Business School professor, Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh. States are starting to feel left out of the windfall, many having granted tax exemptions before the boom. Years ago, before artificial intelligence prompted a tsunami of building, states typically welcomed data centers supporting internet traffic, offering tax abatements and other perks. Many officials now are rethinking that approach as tax revenues take a bigger hit and high energy demands take a toll on affordability. Nevada , for instance, trimmed tax abatements and will ask data centers to agree to foot the bill for energy and water demands, in a September executive order from Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo. States where data center costs will be concentrated over the three years are Texas ($638 billion), Virginia ($249 billion), Ohio ($169 billion) and Georgia ($160 billion), according to projections from Industrial Info Resources, a market intelligence firm. Southern states dominate the landscape for the number of data centers planned, with large numbers also proposed in Arizona, California, Florida, Indiana, Iowa, Indiana, North Carolina, Oregon, Pennsylvania and Washington state, according to a Pew Research Center report in April. The profitability of AI has yet to catch up with the expense of the buildout. “It is not a pretty picture right now,” said IIR’s senior vice president of research, David Pickering. “I think it will become profitable once things settle down a bit and more legislation is put in place to regulate how we handle AI. “The big players will no doubt find a way to make it profitable,” he said. There are signs the staggering cost of data centers is crowding out other investments such as housing. Over the past two years new construction value for data centers has more than doubled to $85 billion annually, while all other construction value has dropped 8%, according to a Stateline analysis of U.S. Census Bureau data as of August. As new data center value grew by $48 billion since 2024, new houses and apartments dropped by $29 billion, according to the data. items.body: A volunteer helps a young person fill out a form on National Voter Registration Day in 2025. For some young voters, abortion remains a defining issue, but for many others it ranks behind more immediate economic concerns. (Photo courtesy of Alliance for Youth Action) Editor’s Note: This story is part of Gen Z at the Ballot Box, a collaboration between States Newsroom and The 19th . Boise State University senior Cade Syvock opposes abortion. As president of the school’s chapter of the conservative group Turning Point USA, the organization founded by the late activist Charlie Kirk, Syvock helped coordinate anti-abortion protests on campus. But he’s not spending much time this fall campaigning against an Idaho ballot initiative that would restore abortion access. Not for lack of interest — he calls the proposed law “very, very extreme” because it allows abortions after viability in certain emergency cases — but because of pressing economic issues he’d rather be working on. “It’s not like everybody’s going out and getting abortions 24/7, but everybody is trying to find a home,” Syvock said. In Idaho and Missouri, where voters will decide the future of abortion access on Nov. 3, campaigns are trying to reach a generation dealing with rising living costs and skepticism toward politics. For some young voters, abortion remains a defining issue. But for many others, it ranks behind more immediate economic concerns. Idaho’s initiative would restore abortion access. Missouri’s measure seeks to reinstate a near-total ban jettisoned by voters two years ago. People pushing for and against both measures are making their appeals to young voters, using social media and canvassing to increase turnout on Election Day, but they’re competing against other issues for Generation Z’s attention. “I’m not saying that the abortion stuff is any less important than housing, but I think in terms of what young people are focusing on right now, it’s definitely dropped a little bit,” Syvock said. Gen Z politicians who want to make a change grapple with parties that aren’t always ready for them In most elections, it’s difficult for campaigns to achieve high turnout among young voters, especially in between presidential election cycles. Less than half of the 40 million Gen Z Americans between ages 18 and 29 who were eligible to vote in 2024 cast a ballot, a study by the Center for Information & Research on Civic Learning and Engagement at Tufts University found. This year, the number of eligible Gen Z-age voters is estimated at nearly 50 million. But there are some signs that turnout could be higher this year. Nonpartisan youth vote organization The Civics Center noted a significant increase in voter registration among 18-year-olds compared with the 2022 midterms, from 35% to 42%. And the Tufts survey points out that there are many signs Gen Z is active and engaged on political subjects, but that connecting issues to candidates and ballot questions is the challenge. The majority of Gen Z adults support abortion access, according to a September poll from The 19th and YouGov. But there’s a gender gap: Women were more likely than men to say abortion should be always or mostly legal, 69% to 51%. Almost half of men versus 31% of women say it should be mostly or always illegal. The number of Generation Z Missourians who got involved in the 2024 initiative petition is not available, but more than 110,000 Idahoans signed the petition to put abortion access on the state ballot. About 7% of those signatures came from people between the ages of 18 and 25, and twice as many of those signatures came from women than from men. But some organizing efforts are made more difficult by local politics as well as increasing costs for food, housing and transportation. The 19th/YouGov poll found that 21% of Gen Z adults were worried about their ability to pay for groceries and 34% were somewhat worried. The attorney general serves a four-year term and receives an annual salary of $146,730. In a Republican-controlled state, Hickman’s election bid faces tough odds. She said she has lived for 30 years in Idaho, where she said her family has deep roots. In 2013, she joined the Boise-based law firm McFarland Ritter as an attorney focusing on business negotiation and litigation. District leaders say the new requirement will ensure compliance with state law governing public school bathroom usage. Multi-occupancy school restrooms must be designated for either males or females and only members of those biological sexes are allowed to enter, as required under Senate Bill 1100 , passed in 2023. “As a public school district, we have a responsibility to comply with Idaho law, regardless of our individual perspectives about it,” Superintendent Scott Woolstenhulme wrote in a letter to employees on Thursday. Idaho law — as established through 2024’s House Bill 421 — also declares that in human beings there are only two sexes, male and female. It was sponsored by Rep. Julianne Young, R-Blackfoot, and Rep. Bruce Skaug, R-Nampa. “An individual’s sex can be observed or clinically verified at or before birth; Rare disorders of sexual development are not exceptions to the binary nature of sex; In no case is an individual’s sex determined by stipulation or self identification,” Idaho law states. Supporters and opponents have raised $9.7 million — so far — in the campaign over Proposition 1, a voter initiative to rescind Idaho’s near-complete abortion ban. Proposition 1 is by far the biggest political battle in the state, and, sensing opportunity, everyone wants a piece of the action. “Both sides are working to mobilize people to vote on that issue,” said Jaclyn Kettler, a political science professor at Boise State University. Proposition 1, explained For a quick and useful overview of what Proposition 1 would do, here’s a summary from Idaho Capital Sun . That also makes Proposition 1 a wild card. The hottest item on the ballot could drive turnout in other Nov. 3 elections — such as the governor’s and the state superintendent’s races; legislative races in Idaho’s scattered swing districts; and the $307 million in school levy requests . The high-powered opposition But for now, let’s focus on Proposition 1 itself. The parochial and partisan opposition is impossible to ignore. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints has contributed $1 million in opposition to Proposition 1 . The Catholic Diocese of Boise has contributed $300,000 . The Idaho Republican Party, meanwhile, has gone all-in against Proposition 1. State GOP chairwoman Dorothy Moon has made the initiative nearly a staple of the weekly op-ed she sends to news outlets; six of her last 10 op-eds mentioned Proposition 1 in whole or in part. Last week, the GOP rolled out a news release touting near unanimous opposition to Proposition 1, from statewide elected officials and Idaho’s congressional delegation. “If there is one issue that unites Republicans across the ideological spectrum, it is that of life,” Moon said. (The only name not on the list: Secretary of State Phil McGrane. Asked about it Tuesday, Moon deferred to McGrane. On Thursday afternoon, McGrane described himself as a pro-life Catholic and a pro-life Republican, but said, as the state’s elections official he is staying neutral on Proposition 1. “It’s important that everyone has confidence in the process,” McGrane told EdNews.) For many Republicans, the Proposition 1 fight is more than just a little personal. After all, the initiative challenges abortion restrictions passed by an overwhelmingly Republican Legislature — and signed into law by Gov. Brad Little, who is seeking a third term next month. Little last week voiced his opposition to Proposition 1, saying it would “make abortion far more accessible in Idaho.” For the state’s prevailing party — and for two of the state’s largest religious groups — fighting Proposition 1 is a matter of seeking to protect the status quo. That alone is a driver, possibly the main one. The down-ticket implications: two recent examples The Republicans’ campaign against Proposition 1 is a marked departure from 2018. And it echoes 2024. (Photo by Clark Corbin/Idaho Capital Sun) Idaho State Department of Agriculture Director Chanel Tewalt told a committee of state legislators Tuesday that she believes Idaho’s population of invasive quagga mussels is very small and confined to limited sections of the Snake River. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE In September 2023, state officials used water sampling to c onfirm the presence of quagga mussel larvae for the first time in state history. During water sampling this year, state officials found eight veliger mussels, the larvae form of the mussels, Tewalt said during a meeting of the Idaho Legislature’s Natural Resources Committee at the Idaho State Capitol in Boise. Scuba divers also found what Tewalt described as “a number of adult mussels” while searching the Snake River. The mussels, which were discovered in the Snake River near Twin Falls, can reproduce extremely rapidly, clog pipes and cover boat hulls. If left unchecked, Tewalt said the spread of quagga mussels poses serious threats to the state’s drinking and irrigation water, recreation industry, state budget and economy. Need to get in touch? Have a news tip? CONTACT US In an effort to completely eradicate all of the invasive species, officials with the Idaho State Department of Agriculture have been administering lethal copper chemicals into the affected part of the Snake River each year since the mussels were first detected. Compared to previous years, the amount of mussels discovered in water sampling is lower and the affected section of the Snake River is smaller this year, Tewalt told legislators. “What it would signify is a very small population,” Tewalt said. After detecting the mussels again this summer, the ag department moved forward with another round of copper-based treatments – with scuba divers injecting the chemicals in harder to reach nooks, crannies and fissures in rock. Chanel Tewalt serves as the director of the Idaho Department of Agriculture. (Courtesy of Idaho State Department of Agriculture) “Copper in the water means that reproduction cycle (for the mussels) is halted,” Tewalt said. Along with mussels, the copper also kills fish and other aquatic life in the river. This year, Tewalt said there have been fewer fish killed and that state officials are not stocking the sections of the river being treated with copper with new fish. Although the mussels were first discovered in water samples in 2023, Tewalt told legislators the mussels have likely been in the Twin Falls pool of the Snake River for longer. Water sampling and monitoring for quagga mussels is an ongoing, years-long process. items.body: Boise State University athletics has the green light to go $18 million in the red. With some reluctance, the State Board of Education approved the deficit spending plan Wednesday afternoon. Most of the $18 million will go into “revenue sharing” — direct payments to student-athletes. And Boise State will use a variety of budget reserves to cover the $18 million. “I personally don’t even like the term … deficit in athletics,” Boise State President David Hahn told State Board members. “Boise State is not running a deficit. We are managing our reserves, we are managing our finances. I’m putting that capital where it needs to be for success of all of the missions.” The $18 million figure is not necessarily unexpected. In August, Boise State Athletic Director Jeramiah Dickey warned the State Board that the cost of revenue sharing — and expenses tied to a move from the Mountain West Conference to a reformed Pac-12 conference — would drive the program into the red. Wednesday’s meeting brought the budget picture into more focus. Boise State is now projecting a $16.9 million deficit for the current budget year, which ends June 30. In August, Dickey pegged this year’s deficit at $14 million to $18 million. The university will provide the athletic department $3 million for debt service. The athletic department hopes to clear $2 million from special events at Albertsons Stadium. The stadium hosted two nights of the Banana Ball baseball barnstorming tour on July 31 and Aug. 1, and country singer Luke Combs is scheduled to perform at Albertsons Stadium on June 12, at the tail end of the budget year. Revenue sharing will increase to about $14.1 million, up from about $10 million. Colleges and universities can spend up to $21.6 million in revenue sharing, and the Boise State payments tie into “overall competitiveness” with rival programs, Dickey told board members. One unknown is the revenue Boise State will collect from the new-look Pac-12, now in its inaugural season. In time, Boise State expects to reap increased revenues from its new conference. But for this year, the university is budgeting for flat conference revenues, unchanged from its final season in the Mountain West, said Stacy Pearson, Boise State’s interim CFO. If the deficit exceeds $18 million, Boise State athletics would have to come back to the State Board for additional spending authority. The State Board approved the deficit spending plan unanimously, but not without discussion. Board member Shawn Keough — a former state senator who co-chaired the Legislature’s budget-writing Joint Finance-Appropriations Committee — said she was “really uncomfortable” with the vote. “I really don’t want to be here in a couple months or another year. Something has to give.” Board President Kurt Liebich said the deficit spending gives Boise State the flexibility it needs during a time of turmoil in college sports. The Senate has passed a college sports overhaul bill , but it is on hold in the House. “(We’re) giving you all the runway you need to figure it out, and I think you guys deserve that runway because of the sustained success you’ve had for 30 years,” said Liebich, who sits on a gubernatorial working group that has been studying the future of Idaho college athletics. Board member David Turnbull described Wednesday’s vote in stark terms. “The option is to basically put a bullet in Bronco sports if we don’t give them this runway.” The State Board is meeting at Lewis-Clark State College through Thursday.

Josh Kohl in the primary, said the three newcomers from District 25 will face a steep learning curve in writing legislation, understanding bills and working with other lawmakers in Boise. “There’s a lot of seniority-based stuff up there, so we’re going to have to work as a coalition to be effective,” Swensen said. We’re committed to working with states on advancing pragmatic AI policies that apply to the entire AI industry — not just one company.” Attorneys general in Arkansas, Montana, Nebraska, West Virginia, Iowa, Kansas and Arizona filed similar lawsuits in their state courts Wednesday, Reuters reported. The Idaho Health Insurers Working Group voted to tee up plans to reform prior auth
items.body: The exterior of the Idaho Statehouse as seen on March 16, 2026, in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) A panel of Idaho lawmakers that studied issues in the health insurance market on Wednesday formalized plans to develop legislation to address a range of issues that affect access to health care. The Idaho Health Insurers Working Group voted to tee up plans to reform prior authorization, a cost-control measure that health insurers use to deny covering certain treatments, and to target several other issues that the interim legislative committee heard about in its meetings in the last few months and through surveys it sent to insurers and health care providers. In a series of votes, the interim committee teed up a series of bills focused on health insurance that could be considered by the Legislature when it returns next January. Some of the other bills that could be drafted could address: Reducing delayed payments to providers, by setting standards for providers and insurers; Establishing uniform standards to credential health care providers through insurers; and Requiring the Idaho Department of Insurance, which regulates health insurers, to collect and present to the Legislature data about the timeliness of payments, and healthcare denial rates. That might also include information on one arbitration tool created by Congress that the state’s largest insurer, Blue Cross of Idaho, claims that a North Idaho microhospital heavily relies upon. Blue Cross argues the practice could drive up the cost of healthcare , and Congress is considering overhauling the tool. The potential prior authorization reform bill wouldn’t be the Legislature’s first attempt to address the issue, which some patients say can delay access to healthcare through drawn out timelines to issue decisions. Earlier this year, a bill, House Bill 611 , set out to require more transparency and establish timelines in the process, but it never received a committee hearing. Rep. Dustin Manwaring, R-Pocatello, listens to proceedings during the Jan. 12, 2026, Joint Finance-Appropriations Committee meeting at the State Capitol Building in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) Prior authorization also impacts healthcare providers. Providers in Idaho reported spending more time on administrative work to respond to prior authorization requests in recent years, according to data that committee co-chairman Rep. Dustin Manwaring, R-Pocatello, summarized. In 2025, an American Medical Association survey found that 92% of physicians reported negative patient impacts caused by prior authorization processes. The committee was formed after a now-resolved contract fallout between a hospital in East Idaho, Portneuf Medical Center, and the insurer that runs the health plan for state employees, Regence BlueShield of Idaho. In the coming years, the state plans to transition Medicaid, a health insurance public assistance program for people who have disabilities or earn low-incomes, from being state-run to being managed by private health insurance companies . items.body: Pocatello-Chubbuck trustees appear inclined to keep the district’s five-day school week after discussing the matter during a board work session Tuesday. The board will vote next week to either stay on a five-day schedule or move to four-day model. The board will also consider swapping the current trimester schedule for semesters. The district began considering these and other changes in June. Four-day weeks have gained popularity across Idaho in recent years. Last school year, about two in three districts used four-day calendars. Eighteen of the state’s 76 charter schools use the model. In 2024, Nampa — similar in size to Pocatello-Chubbuck — became Idaho’s largest district to join the trend, which is most common among smaller districts. Pocatello-Chubbuck trustees favor five-day week Trustees Heather Clarke, Megan Furniss, Deanna Judy and Bill Osborn said they would vote to maintain the five-day week in Pocatello because of concerns a four-day week would negatively impact learning and be a difficult change for staff. Furniss pointed to families who rely on the district’s social services. Only a quarter of families with children who qualify for free and reduced-price lunch responded to a recent four-day week survey, she said, creating a “gaping hole” in the results. A survey of parents and district employees with 2,700 respondents found a split in community opinion: 56%, or about 1,500 respondents, said a four-day week is ideal. “In the end, public education is intended to serve every student,” not just families who can arrange childcare on Fridays, Furniss said. Osborn pointed to numbers showing that just 2% of schools nationwide are on a four-day week, convincing him that the five-day week is better. Judy called a switch “a huge jump.” She spoke about a hybrid model where students attend school two Fridays a month, but Clarke repeatedly objected, saying it wasn’t the purpose of the workshop. Meanwhile, Clarke, Furniss and Board Chair Raymond Knoff said they prefer the district’s current trimester system over semesters. Furniss cited students’ abilities to take more electives in an academic year. The board will also vote on the trimester-semester option next week. Other business Trustees also discussed a survey of more than 2,000 Pocatello-Chubbuck high school students regarding their preferred career-technical education (CTE) offerings. Culinary arts, welding and health professions were the most popular among students. Seventy-eight percent of students said it is important that their electives connect to future career pathways. Much of trustees’ discussion centered on military science, one of the least popular options on the survey. Pocatello Director of Business Jonathan Balls also presented the board with a summary of completed facilities maintenance projects, including an update on the Highland High School rebuild project. The school caught fire and saw severe damage in 2023.

items.body: The groups opposing and supporting Proposition 1, the proposed abortion rights initiative that will be on the Nov. 3 general election ballot, collected more than $2.5 million total in just under two weeks. (Photo illustration by Getty Images) The political action committee opposing Idaho’s Proposition 1 abortion rights initiative collected nearly $1.5 million since the end of September, buoyed by two large donations from churches. The Too Extreme for Idaho PAC, reported the previously announced $1 million donation from the Salt Lake City-based Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints on Oct. 8. The Roman Catholic Diocese of Boise donated another $300,000 to the PAC opposing the initiative the next day. Supporters and opponents of Idaho’s abortion rights initiative, Prop 1, have raised millions Since Sept. 29, Too Extreme for Idaho received $153,985 from 32 individual people and $1.3 million from four organizations, including the two churches. Too Extreme for Idaho has raised a total of just over $4 million, campaign finance data shows. As of Monday, the PAC supporting the initiative, Idahoans United for Women and Families, brought in more than $630,000 since Sept. 29. The largest donation came from the federal Government that Works PAC, based out of Washington, D.C, which gave $250,000. Oklahoma-based billionaire philanthropist Lynn Schusterman donated $200,000 on Sept. 30, campaign finance data shows. Since Sept. 29, the PAC received $265,290 from 81 individuals and $370,000 from three organizations. In total, Idahoans United has collected more than $5.6 million. Independent expenditures for and against Prop 1 total more than $2.5 million Groups and individuals spent more than $2.5 million combined to support and oppose Prop 1 in independent expenditures, which includes spending by organizations or individuals spent directly to support or oppose a ballot measure. The Idaho Secretary of State’s office in late September and early October began sharing a message with those filing campaign finance reports to request that any spending for or against a ballot initiative, constitutional amendment or advisory question be reported as an independent expenditure to help “voters more easily find and understand spending related to ballot measures.” The notice, first uploaded to the campaign finance reporting portal the last week of September and then updated on Oct. 7, also asked filers to amend previous campaign finance reports to classify spending related to ballot measures as independent expenditures. This request is likely why this category of election spending seemed to jump significantly from a previous Idaho Capital Sun analysis of campaign spending data . 2026 Voter Guide Dates to know, how-to instructions and candidate surveys for Idaho’s top contested races. The anti-abortion group Right to Life Idaho PAC also reported spending more than $17,600 on advertising regarding the ballot measure, but reported its position as “N/A” in its campaign finance disclosure report. The same PAC reported a little over $1,000 in opposition to the measure, campaign finance data shows. Too Extreme for Idaho led independent expenditure spending with over $1.2 million spent in opposition. Idaho Chooses Life also reported spending more than $66,000 to oppose the initiative. items.body: The Idaho Department of Lands managed the Tyson Fire, which firefighters responded to in Benewah County in July 2023. (Photo courtesy of the Idaho Department of Lands) More than 80% of the wildfires that the Idaho Department of Lands has responded to this year have been caused by humans, Director Dustin Miller told an interim committee of Idaho legislators Tuesday. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE “This staggering figure just underscores the importance of not only a robust fuels mitigation program … but also a solid prevention program,” Miller told the Idaho Legislature’s Natural Resources Interim Committee during a meeting at the Idaho State Capitol in Boise. Through the end of September, a total of 10,000 acres of land that the Idaho Department of Lands is responsible for protecting has burned. (That figure does not include the larger number of acres of federal land, such as U.S. Forest Service land, that burned in wildfires this summer.) Dustin Miller is the director of the Idaho Department of Lands. (Photo courtesy of the Idaho Department of Lands) The increase in human-caused fires is not new. In 2023, Miller also told a commission of statewide elected officials that he was investigating a spike in human-caused fires , the Idaho Capital Sun previously reported. Miller told state legislators the costs of wildfires are high, and several legislators immediately pushed for more answers. Through the end of September, the state’s wildfire costs were a little over $47 million, of which an estimated $19.8 million could be reimbursable from other agencies the state partners with, Miller said. In addition to the financial cost to taxpayers, fires also can also threaten the safety of firefighters and the public, destroy property and burn state endowment timber lands that generate funding for public schools and other beneficiaries. There is also the cost of rehabilitation and recovery following fire and the long-term effects caused by fire. Idaho legislators ask how state can recoup costs for human-caused fires While human-caused fires aren’t new, the 80% figure grabbed the attention of several legislators. Senate Majority Leader Lori Den Hartog, R-Meridian, asked Miller if the state was doing enough to go after the people who were responsible. Natural Resources Interim Committee Co-Chair Britt Raybould, R-Rexburg, asked if stronger penalties would be a deterrent. “Just something that encourages people to think a little more responsibly about how their behavior can have, not only the financial, but the environmental and property damage and all of the surrounding consequences,” Raybould said. State Rep. Britt Raybould, R-Rexburg, speaks from the floor of the Idaho House of Representatives on March 16, 2026, at the Idaho Capitol Building in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) Miller told the committee that the state investigates the cause of every fire and attempts to recoup funding from individuals or groups that are deemed “negligent.” Sometimes the recovery process works well, Miller said, but sometimes it can take years to recover the money, and the state doesn’t always succeed. “Oftentimes we settle for less than what the suppression costs were,” Miller said. “We really try to work with the individual and their insurance companies,” Miller added. “These are taxpayers always, and we want to recoup as much as we can back to the general taxpayer. But you know, we have been fairly successful.” During a break in Tuesday’s meeting, Miller told the Sun the causes of the fires include people losing control of their burning debris piles, sparks caused by chains or other metal equipment, discarded cigarette butts, escaped camp fires that were never fully extinguished and more. items.body: (UPDATED, 6:34 p.m., with open letter from Boise trustees and administrators.) The Boise School District is launching an internal investigation into reported online death threats against a student. Details on the district’s Timberline High School investigation are unclear. “We cannot disclose individual student discipline due to student privacy requirements,” district spokesman Dan Hollar said in an email to Idaho EdNews. The district had put its investigation on hold while waiting on the Boise Police Department. Police finished their interviews Wednesday, “and we were … given the all clear to begin investigating on our own,” Boise district Area Director Shelley Bonds told the Boise School Board Monday evening. The Boise police investigation is ongoing, spokeswoman Haley Kramer told EdNews Tuesday morning. “We have completed the initial essential interviews, preserved immediately available evidence, and requested preservation of additional evidence not yet received.” Police were brought in on the investigation on Oct. 2, the day the threats were reported to school and district officials. According to an online petition, members of the Timberline football team went on the Snapchat social media site and talked about raping and killing a female student. Boise police increased their presence at the school last week. District and school officials postponed some homecoming activities and canceled a homecoming football game scheduled for Thursday , citing concerns about student safety. Hundreds of Timberline students staged a walkout during classes Wednesday . Students demonstrate in front of Timberline High in Boise on Wednesday, Oct. 7, 2026. items.body: Voters cast their ballots in the primary election on May 21, 2024, at Linden Park Elementary School in Idaho Falls. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) 2026 Voter Guide The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote. Read More As the 2026 Nov. 3 general election approaches, Idahoans have been asking questions about filling out ballots, write-in candidates, online voter registration searches, and more as they gear up to vote. The Idaho Capital Sun spoke to Secretary of State Phil McGrane and his staff about some of the top concerns that have arisen this election season. Here are some of the most frequently asked questions: If I don’t fill in a response to every question, does my ballot still count? Idaho Secretary of State Phil McGrane attends the State of the State Address at the State Capitol building in Boise on Jan. 8, 2024. (Otto Kitsinger for Idaho Capital Sun) Voters can skip any question or race on their ballot if they choose to. McGrane had heard concerns from voters worried that if they didn’t fill out a response to one of the ballot questions, that the rest of their ballot would be thrown out. This won’t happen, he said. “Voters are not required to vote in every race on their ballot for it to count,” the secretary of state’s office spokesperson Joe Parris said in an email. “If they skip a question or contest, the remaining selections on their ballot will still be counted.” Can I write in a candidate or write in an answer to the state gun advisory question? Prospective write-in candidates in Idaho must file a “Declaration of Intent” to run with the Idaho Secretary of State’s Office, and the deadline to do so was Sept. 4. Voters may still write in a name, but that vote won’t count if it doesn’t go toward a registered write-in candidate. This year, the only write-in candidate who filed this declaration is independent gubernatorial candidate Jacob Burnett, according to the Secretary of State’s Office. For House Joint Resolution 4 , House Joint Resolution 6 , and Proposition 1 , there are only “yes” or “no” options to fill out on the ballot. The advisory question about selecting an official state gun has six choices of gun and no option to write in a response. Are signatures on absentee ballots verified, and how? Signatures on all absentee ballots are verified, Idaho Secretary of State’s Office officials said. Election staff members compare signatures on the ballots with voter registration, signature history on previous ballots, and driver’s license records to confirm a match before ballots are counted, Parris said. “Make sure you sign your own absentee ballot,” Parris said. “A common mistake is a spouse putting their return ballot in the wrong return ballot envelope.” GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE I can’t find my voter registration. Have I been purged from the voter rolls? Voters who have moved, changed their name or haven’t voted in the past four years will need to update their voter registration. Eligible voters who are still having a hard time finding their voter information in the Secretary of State’s online voter look-up tool at VoteIdaho.Gov may be running into the tool’s more stringent search requirement. “No one’s being removed,” McGrane said. “It’s our search function on VoteIdaho(.gov) got tighter, and so we’ve been working to try and resolve it.” The tool was previously updated after several people were unable to find their voter registration and expressed concern that they’d been removed from the voter rolls, the Idaho Capital Sun reported. The issue was previously linked to people searching on their cellphones, but other voters have run into challenges finding their information. “Voters need to use their name exactly as they registered it,” Parris said. “If a user, for example, registered as ‘Elizabeth,’ the short name ‘Beth’ won’t yield results. items.body: All three candidates for Idaho’s top education job say that the state should be more transparent about who’s benefiting from a fledgling private school choice program. Incumbent state superintendent Debbie Critchfield, a Republican, faced challengers Becky Sundin Mitchell, a Democrat, and Teresa Roundy of the Constitution Party in a live, televised debate Monday. Idaho News 6, a Boise-based TV station, hosted the debate. The candidates agreed on many topics during the hourlong event, including whether the state should release data that shows how many recipients of the Parental Choice Tax Credit were previously enrolled in private school. They also agreed that private schools receiving taxpayer funds should be subject to similar academic reporting requirements as public schools. “It’s no different than any other government program that is funded through taxpayer dollars,” Critchfield said. “We have an expectation to know where those dollars go.” Critchfield added that the state should find out whether parents are satisfied with the education choices that they made for their children. The tax credit offers families up to $5,000 — or $7,500 if they have a disability — to offset private school tuition and other nonpublic education expenses, including homeschooling costs. Since the program launched Jan. 15, the Idaho State Tax Commission, the state agency responsible for administering the tax credit, has yet to release data that would test a key selling point of the program: that it would help students who couldn’t otherwise afford private education. “Any time that taxpayer money is used for anything, there should be accountability attached to it,” Sundin Mitchell said. “I’m concerned that we passed this tax credit system without having any accountability measures in place.” Roundy agreed. “The state should track and publicly report these figures to ensure total transparency, fiscal responsibility and equity for Idaho taxpayers,” she said. “Public funds must be used effectively and should never subsidize the wealthy at the expense of families who are genuinely struggling.” Idaho News 6 senior reporter Riley Shoemaker and neighborhood reporters Greenlee Clark and Allie Triepke moderated the debate. Candidates were given one minute to respond to each question. The candidates also discussed Idaho’s aging school funding formula, school security, facilities funding and special education, among other topics. Click here to watch the full debate. items.body: Idaho’s colleges and universities are seeking more than $170 million for capital projects — requests likely to far outstrip available funding. The money would come from the Permanent Building Fund, which receives a share of lottery dividends and collects a host of tax carveouts. The fund pays for public works projects across state government, not just on campuses. This year’s Permanent Building Fund budget came to $72.5 million. Gov. Brad Little and the Legislature cut into this budget, siphoning $48.5 million in interest earnings into a cash-strapped state general fund budget. Consequently, the state funded only $890,000 for a single capital project this year, an Idaho National Guard request. State agencies requested $229.4 million for capital requests, and most were unfunded. Nonetheless, when Idaho college and university leaders appeared before the Permanent Building Fund’s advisory council Tuesday, they took turns pitching a long list of capital projects. Here’s a closer look at the higher education requests: College of Western Idaho . The state’s largest two-year college has the longest and costliest wish list in the higher education system. items.body: The Professional Standards Commission approved disciplinary actions for five Idaho educators earlier this month. The state commission oversees educator certification and investigates potential violations of Idaho’s educator ethics code. It can impose discipline on an educator’s certificate, including suspension or revocation. Here’s a closer look at the latest disciplinary actions and the educators involved. Revocations Wesley Naylor , Richfield School District Ethics violations: Not maintaining a professional relationship with students Disciplinary action: Certificate revoked In September 2025, Naylor grabbed a student’s arm and/or pushed them as they tried to walk out of the classroom after the student ignored Naylor. Naylor pleaded guilty to disturbing the peace related to the incident in December 2025. Casey Hood , Arizona Ethics violations: Failing to exemplify honesty and integrity in the course of professional practice Disciplinary action: Certificate revoked Hood surrendered her Arizona teaching certificate for five years starting in September 2025 after allegations that she modified expired individualized education plans to make it appear that required meetings had occurred when they had not. Note: Educators listed without a school district were likely not working at an Idaho school when their ethics violations occurred, though they either held or applied for an Idaho certification at some point. Suspension Michael Robert Driscoll, Boise Ethics violations: Failure to refrain from the abuse of alcohol or drugs during the course of professional practice Disciplinary action: Suspension of certificate until completion of an alcohol recovery program In August 2025, a fellow staff member reported that Driscoll smelled like alcohol and had a cup in his classroom with a liquid that also smelled like alcohol. Driscoll was removed from the classroom. He refused an alcohol test, but the liquid in the cup tested positive for alcohol. Driscoll agreed to the disciplinary action, which requires him to complete an alcohol recovery program to get his license reinstated. Letters of reprimand Jessica Bailey, St. Maries Ethics violations: Failed to maintain a professional relationship with students Disciplinary action: Letter of reprimand and completion of an approved-boundaries course Bailey was accused of crossing professional boundaries with a student by being alone with one of them in a classroom without an educational purpose. She exchanged texts with a student that were unrelated to school instruction or responsibilities, including plans to spend time together doing recreational activities and for the student to help with a project at Bailey’s home. Bailey agreed to the disciplinary action. Cheryl Griebenow, Caldwell Ethics violations: Did not fulfill all terms and obligations detailed in the contract with the local school board of education or education agency for the duration of the contract. Disciplinary action: Letter of reprimand Griebenow submitted a letter of resignation in November 2025, which the board of trustees did not accept the following month. Because she was not released from her contract, Griebenow was found to be in violation of the code of ethics. Griebenow agreed to the disciplinary action.

items.body: Boise State University officials on Friday cut the ribbon on the new ESI Construction Management facility, built to serve one of the university’s fastest-growing programs. It’s not just a building, said Anthony Perrenoud, the program’s department chair. It’s a tool for learning. Many of the building’s features are interactive, helping students learn how to assemble a structure. Growth in the Construction Management program was also a factor. “When we designed this building, there were 300 students” in the program, Perrenoud said. Now, it has 560 students. Inside the building The ESI Construction Management building stands out on campus for its extensive use of wood. Wood products company Boise Cascade donated the timber for the project, which is the first mass-timber building on campus. The facility includes student workspaces, a computer lab, classrooms and conference rooms. It also has a 3,300-square-foot “high bay” — a giant garage — with an overhead crane and an outdoor learning area. The state controller is a constitutional officer that serves as Idaho’s chief fiscal officer and serves on the Idaho State Board of Land Commissioners, which is commonly referred to as the Land Board. The position is for a four-year term and comes with an annual salary of $128,690. Meet Democratic challenger Rakesh Mohan Mohan worked as a government auditor and evaluator for 36 years, working for state legislatures in Idaho, Washington, Louisiana and Kansas. He spent the last 21 years of his evaluation career as director of the nonpartisan Idaho Office of Performance Evaluations until he retired in June 2024 . After that, Mohan served as a visiting professor at the School of Public Policy at Boise State University. Mohan is not an accountant or IT professional, but he said his 30-plus years of experience evaluating and auditing government policy and programs has prepared him to serve as controller. He said he is running because he believes in accountability and transparency and did not want to see Woolf run unopposed, like Woolf did in the 2014 and 2018 general elections. “Since I decided to run and I started talking to people, the very first questions I get asked are, ‘Do we have a controller? But if people don’t even know we exist, then what kind of transparency do we have here?” Rakesh Mohan Mohan said he views the controller’s job as looking over taxpayer dollars that go to the state. The job also includes overseeing payroll for all state employees and making sure the right amount of money goes to the right place at the right time. Mohan said the office is responsible for statewide accounting and the state’s large data systems. “It may sound boring to most people, but it is an extremely important job,” Mohan said. “And the controller is also responsible for paying all the bills. items.body: Idaho Education News’ board of directors announced today CEO Jennifer Swindell has been named publisher and Devin Bodkin has been named COO and managing editor of the nonprofit, online news organization. Swindell founded Idaho EdNews in January of 2013 and has served as CEO and managing editor over its 14-year development. She will continue to serve as the company’s CEO. Jennifer Swindell, Idaho EdNews founder and publisher “Jennifer is an extraordinary leader and journalist,” said EdNews Board Chair Alicia Ritter. “This promotion is recognition of her success at growing an organization whose consistent and solid news reporting has elevated thoughtful and impactful discussion of education in Idaho.” Bodkin spent the last year as EdNews’ assistant managing editor, prepping for today’s promotion. Previously, he was an East Idaho reporter, blogger and editor for EdNews. He will continue to work and live in eastern Idaho. “We’re lucky to have a talent like Devin take the reins of EdNews management,” Ritter said. “His experience, talent and perspective will serve readers well as he steps into big shoes.” Swindell is an award-winning investigative journalist and editor and has been an Idaho journalist for nearly 40 years. She spent 20 years at the Idaho Statesman as a reporter, columnist and editor. She also was a director of communications for Boise State University before launching EdNews. As publisher, Swindell will set the strategic vision of Idaho EdNews and continue to be the public face of the organization. Bodkin previously was a corporate editor at the Idaho National Laboratory and a former Idaho teacher. As managing editor, he will be responsible for day-to-day operations. EdNews, a non-profit, is governed by a three-person board, including Ritter. Also serving on the board are Kim O’Connor, a former journalist and victim witness coordinator for the Ada County Prosecutor’s Office, and Stacia Albiston, a former teacher and the communications officer for the J.A. and Kathryn Albertson Family Foundation. Devin Bodkin, Idaho EdNews COO and managing editor In other staff news, Ryan Suppe is being promoted to accountability reporter and assistant managing editor. He’ll pursue watchdog stories and assist Bodkin with day-to-day operations. Suppe was EdNews’ politics reporter. Sean Dolan will move into the politics reporter position and cover the Idaho Legislature with veteran reporter Kevin Richert, who has covered the Legislature for more than 35 years with the Idaho Statesman and Idaho Education News. Richert also will continue to write his Thursday analysis pieces and anchor the new Idaho EdNews Show, a regular podcast-video. Emma Epperly will continue to serve as EdNews North Idaho reporter, rounding out a team whose reporting reaches all corners of the state. She also follows charter school development and how policies are implemented in Idaho schools. EdNews has won multiple national and statewide awards for investigative and watchdog journalism. The website has seen record growth this past year, reaching millions of page views and social media followers. EdNews produces comprehensive and thoughtful journalism about education policy and practice in Idaho. The nonprofit is a public awareness service where parents, patrons, educators and lawmakers can find the most useful information on issues that affect Idaho’s children and their future. EdNews is committed to its mission of holding lawmakers and educators accountable for taxpayer dollars and student achievement. EdNews is free and published without advertising thanks to the generosity of the J.A. and Kathryn Albertson Family Foundation. For questions or comments, contact Jennifer at jswindell@idahoednews.org . items.body: The Boise Temple of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints as seen on Feb. 5, 2025. (Photo by Otto Kitsinger for Idaho Capital Sun) The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints has donated $1 million to an Idaho political action committee, or PAC, opposing the abortion rights initiative on the ballot this November. The donation went to the Too Extreme for Idaho Political Action Committee, which opposes the initiative. “While The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints remains neutral toward political candidates, it actively addresses ballot initiatives it believes carry significant moral consequences,” the church said in a statement. “Accordingly, the Church has joined a coalition of like-minded organizations and individuals in Idaho to dedicate resources toward defeating Proposition 1.” Supporters and opponents of Idaho’s abortion rights initiative, Prop 1, have raised millions If passed, the voter initiative would repeal Idaho’s abortion laws, enumerate rights related to reproductive health, and create liability protections for healthcare providers who provide abortion and other reproductive healthcare. The Idaho Falls radio station NewsTalk 107.9 first reported the donation on Thursday. The Idaho Capital Sun confirmed the donation with a spokesperson for the church on Friday. The large donation comes after Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador published an opinion in August that says churches are allowed to donate money to political campaigns — including for and against Proposition 1 — without disclosing their donors, as long as they don’t ask members to donate specifically for the campaign, Boise State Public Radio reported. Leaders from the church, widely known as the Mormon church, issued a letter against Prop 1 in September, the Salt Lake Tribune reported. The letter was read to congregations last month, the church’s assistant communications director Brian Whitlock said in an email. “Our long-held stance on abortion remains clear and unchanged,” the four-member U.S. Central Area Presidency of the LDS Church wrote in the letter. The church, which opposes elective abortions, posted its stance on abortion online . It allows for possible exemptions in cases of rape and incest, or in cases where a “competent physician determines that the life or health of the mother is in serious jeopardy,” or a “competent physician determines that the fetus has severe defects that will not allow the baby to survive beyond birth.” “Even these exceptions do not automatically justify abortion,” the statement said. “Abortion is a most serious matter. items.body: President Donald Trump signed an executive order to allow dyed diesel on highways and prohibit the Internal Revenue Service from imposing the typical penalties for doing so. Some state restrictions remain on the fuel, but on Friday, Idaho Gov. Brad Little relaxed the Gem State's inspections of the fuel during harvest. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor) Idaho Gov. Brad Little signed an executive order Friday to suspend for 30 days state inspections of dyed diesel fuel in an attempt to lower costs for farmers and ranchers, according to the governor’s office. With election pressure mounting, states move to suspend fuel taxes Dyed diesel is diesel fuel with red dye in it and is exempt from federal and state motor fuel taxes. The tax-exempt fuel is only meant for certain approved off-road uses, such as for farming equipment, construction equipment and home heating. The dye helps regulators enforce this requirement. Idaho’s average diesel price was around $6.41 per gallon as of Friday, according to AAA fuel prices. Prices for oil products have risen this year largely because of restrictions on ships passing through the Strait of Hormuz amid the U.S. and Israel’s war with Iran, which have disrupted global supply chains. Diesel supplies have been in particularly short supply, NPR reported, and Ukraine’s attacks on Russian refineries have also affected global supplies. On Monday, President Donald Trump signed an executive order to allow dyed diesel on highways and prohibit the Internal Revenue Service from imposing the typical penalties for doing so. Some state restrictions remain on the fuel. President Donald Trump hands off a newly signed executive order waiving federal taxes on red-dyed diesel to aide Natalie Harp during a 2026 midterms rally in Grand Island, Nebraska, on Oct. 5, 2026, at the Nebraska State Fairgrounds with thousands in attendance. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner) Little’s order signed Friday directs Idaho State Police and the Idaho Transportation Department to suspend inspection for dyed diesel while the agencies review Idaho’s policies and procedures, his office announced in a press release. The review will consider other state’s approach to dyed diesel enforcement and the agencies will make recommendations to Little for “efficient, effective, and practical inspection,” the release said. Little said in the press release that the timing of the order is meant to ease costs during harvest season. “Idaho farmers and ranchers work hard to feed our families, our country, and the world,” Little said in the release. “President Trump has made cutting red tape a priority, and Idaho is doing the same. We will continue looking for ways to give our farmers, ranchers, and working men and women on the road more freedom to do what they do best.” Legislative leaders in written statements said they supported the governor’s decision. “Idaho farmers and ranchers are facing high costs across the board, and expensive diesel is adding to the pressure during harvest,” Senate President Pro Tempore Kelly Anthon, R-Declo, said in the release. “This order provides some immediate relief while giving the state time to review these requirements and find a practical approach that supports our producers without adding unnecessary costs or red tape.” House Speaker Mike Moyle , R-Star, said suspending the inspections while the state reviews its policies “is a practical approach that puts common sense first and gives Idaho producers one less thing to worry about during harvest.” YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE. Idaho Republican Gov. Brad Little gives his State of the State Address from the House chambers on Jan. 12, 2026, at the State Capitol Building in Boise. Through the first three months of Fiscal Year 2027, state revenues are now up by $90.3 million, or 6.8%. The surging revenues in this year’s state budget are a stark contrast to last year, when Little and Idaho state legislators approved near across-the-board budget cuts for almost all state agencies, programs and departments to pay for federal tax cuts President Donald Trump signed into law through the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and to ensure the state passed a balanced budget, the Idaho Capital Sun previously reported. State revenues were also up in July and August. “Idaho’s strong revenue growth is encouraging and reflects the strength of our economy, but we must remain disciplined and make spending decisions based on what we can responsibly sustain,” Little said in a written statement Friday afternoon. “The difficult decisions we made last year put us in a stronger fiscal position, and we need to continue prioritizing the investments that matter most to Idahoans while protecting our long-term financial stability.” Income tax withholdings are driver of state revenue increase Individual income tax withholdings are a big part of the revenue increase. The September General Fund Revenue Report said individual income tax collections are up 18.3% fiscal year to date. “It appears that employees are getting lots of hours of work and that there may be some bonus activity being paid by employers,” Idaho Division of Financial Management officials wrote in the September revenue report. items.title: GOP consistently cuts mental health investments
items.summary: The mental health of our children is on everyone’s mind, including school leaders. That’s why 10 rural districts and charter schools jumped at the chance to apply for mental health support through Idaho’s Rural Health Transformation Program. items.body: The mental health of our children is on everyone’s mind, including school leaders. That’s why 10 rural districts and charter schools jumped at the chance to apply for mental health support through Idaho’s Rural Health Transformation Program. The plans included counseling, telehealth, and behavioral health coordinators to help students and families connect with care. Their work was wasted when a Republican-only interim committee voted to shut down the opportunity and redirect $1.2 million. The documented need was high. In Notus, 46% of surveyed junior high and high school students identified mental health as a concern, and the district sought $60,000 for a coordinator serving students from preschool through 12th grade. Aberdeen wanted to expand counseling and wellness services in a community where some care is 20 to 50 minutes away. The decision is hard to understand, but it fits a pattern from the Republican supermajority: cutting investments in mental health. Last year, Idaho eliminated Assertive Community Treatment, or ACT, along with peer support services, as years of tax cuts for the wealthy left less money for essential services. ACT provided intensive, mobile care for people with severe mental illness. Providers and law enforcement warned that people would end up in crisis without those supports. Soon, visits to eastern Idaho crisis centers had increased by 34% in December and 43% in January compared with the year before. Providers reported rising hospitalizations and more pressure on jails. Four former ACT patients died after the program was cut, compared with one reported death during the previous 18 months. After months of warnings and advocacy from mental health practitioners, lawmakers pieced together one-time funding to bring ACT and peer support back. That meant providers had to fight to restore services instead of focusing on patients in their communities. But the future of those services remains uncertain. These cuts were not just cruel. They were shortsighted from a budget perspective, too. Providers estimated ACT cost less than $100 per patient per day, while untreated illness can lead to repeated hospitalizations, court hearings, and jail stays that cost taxpayers far more. When elected officials disregard the health and safety of our communities, there should be accountability. The Rural Health Transformation Committee is made up of eight Republican lawmakers, including Reps. Dori Healey and Dustin Manwaring. Both are now up for reelection in two of the most competitive legislative districts in Idaho. Voters in those districts should take a hard look at this record. Blocking mental health resources for rural families after Idaho has already seen the consequences of cutting care is the kind of decision that should carry real political consequences. The Republicans who made this decision had the chance to learn from what happened. Now voters do too.

items.body: The Idaho Public Charter School Commission approved applications for two new schools Thursday — with some conditions. Elevate Academy, a network of career-technical charters, is also preparing a new CTE-focused school serving grades 6-12 in Pocatello. items.body: Boise State University’s 10-year campus master plan has buy-in at City Hall. The Boise City Council signed off Tuesday on the university’s land use plan, the Idaho Statesman reported . This vote links the university’s plan and the city’s comprehensive land use plan. The 10-year university plan is designed to accommodate projected growth at Idaho’s largest four-year university — by adding 750 dormitory beds, 370 parking spaces and 270 staff members. The top priority is a $140 million science research building, a 90,000- to 110,000-square-foot project that would go up on the southern fringe of campus. Designed to address the university’s shortage of research space, the new building is scheduled to come online in 2029. The dorm space will focus on two areas of need: housing for first-year students and graduate student housing. City Hall will still get a say on specific projects. “While we’re approving a master plan, we’re not approving any specific plans,” said council member Jimmy Hallyburton, according to a Statesman report on the Tuesday meeting. “Those things would have to come back before council.” More reading: Click here for an in-depth April article on Boise State’s 10-year plan.

items.body: For 80 minutes Tuesday night, Terri Pickens and John Stegner agreed about almost everything. Especially Brad Little. Sharing a stage at a Boise junior high school auditorium, Pickens and Stegner took turns laying out a litany of criticisms. Little is too deferential to President Donald Trump. Little compromises too much with House Speaker Mike Moyle and other conservative lawmakers. Little is wrong on private school choice. Wrong about opening Idaho to, potentially, thousands of tons of nuclear waste shipments . Weak on public lands. Too often silent. Pickens, an attorney, and Stegner, a retired judge, presented a case for the prosecution. An audience of about 150 people murmured their approval, applauded on occasion, and snickered at the zingers. Little provided no defense. The two-term governor was a no-show for the League of Women Voters forum . A folding chair, reserved for Little, sat vacant. A bottle of water remained unopened.
