items.body: Voters cast their ballots during the May 19, 2026, primary election at The Waterfront in Idaho Falls. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) This year, Idaho voters have a lot to decide on: Who will be the state’s next governor or U.S. senator? Should two constitutional amendments pass? Should voters pass their own law to repeal the state’s abortion ban? 2026 Voter Guide Dates to know, how-to instructions and candidate surveys for Idaho’s top contested races. Read More But in the mix is a poll that the Idaho Legislature called for: What should be the state’s official gun? Idaho, a Republican supermajority-controlled state, has strong protections for gun ownership — such as not requiring permits for concealed carry in city limits. The state Legislature considered a bill this year to allow members of the public to carry concealed guns inside parts of courthouses that aren’t meant for court, like offices for county commissioners and clerks. The advisory question on the ballot this year asks voters to weigh in on the Legislature’s possible decision to declare a firearm — out of a mix of well-known Western and American guns — as Idaho’s official state gun. If Idaho declared a state gun, the recognition would grow the list of officially declared state symbols , like the state flower, the syringa; the state gem, the star garnet; or the state amphibian, the Idaho giant salamander. Ten other states have declared state guns , according to the National Rifle Association, a prominent gun lobbying group. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE Idaho lawmaker hopes the advisory question will boost voter turnout One of the lawmakers behind the push for the ballot question, Rep. Jason Monks, R-Meridian, said he thought it might drum up voter turnout during a year when many consequential issues are on the ballot. In election years when the president isn’t on the ballot, like this year, fewer voters tend to participate. “Voter turnout is always important,” he said in an interview. “… When you have a lot of voter apathy, I think we don’t get as good of results as we could if we had an informed electorate that was actually out and voting.” The votes won’t be the final say. “The results,” the bill says, “will guide the Legislature as to which gun shall be designated the state gun of Idaho.” Idaho Senate Majority Leader Lori Den Hartog, R-Meridian, and Idaho House Majority Leader Jason Monks, R-Meridian, walk Gov. Brad Little out of the House chambers after the governor delivered his State of the State Address on Jan. 12, 2026, at the State Capitol Building in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) But Monks said this is the only time he knows of when the state sought public input before designating a state item. Monks acknowledges that not everyone loves the idea of declaring a state gun. “I don’t think you can make everybody always happy. The majority of people in Idaho do have guns,” he said. “We have a pretty high percentage of gun ownership in our state. And so I think it reflects the fact that Idaho is a very gun-friendly state, and that it is an important part of our culture in many aspects.” He stressed that the push for the ballot question didn’t take much time. “I had some people ask me, ‘How come this is your priority?’ I’m like, ‘Well, this isn’t my priority. It’s just something we did kind of on the side,’” Monks said. “I put in 12 to 14 hour days there all the time, and I can tell you I spent very little time on this particular issue. items.body: U.S. Attorney for the District of Idaho Bart Davis in his Boise office. (Photo by Laura Guido/Idaho Capital Sun) Idaho’s top-ranking federal law enforcement official, U.S. Attorney Bart Davis, announced his retirement Wednesday following a long, influential legal and political career in Idaho . ‘The best job I ever had’: Bart Davis returns as Idaho’s chief federal litigator Davis, who is 71 and in his second term as U.S. attorney for the District of Idaho, will retire Oct. 17, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Idaho said. “I am unable to overstate the privilege it has been to work with the dedicated and remarkable women and men of the U.S. Attorney’s Office,” Davis said in a written statement. “These great lawyers and support staff faithfully enforce the law, work to keep Idaho and our country safe, support our law enforcement partners and protect the civil rights of others. I am proud of the work they do every day.” President Donald Trump nominated Davis for U.S. attorney for the District of Idaho last year, and the U.S. Senate confirmed Davis on Oct. 7, 2025 – exactly one year before Davis announced his retirement. Davis previously served as U.S. attorney for the District of Idaho from 2017 to 2021 during Trump’s first term. Prior to serving as U.S. attorney, Davis practiced law in Idaho Falls and served in the Idaho Senate for 19 years. Davis, a Republican, served as Senate majority leader for 15 years, where he was regarded as a powerful and intelligent legislative leader. “Bart Davis has served the State of Idaho and our country with distinction throughout a remarkable career,” Idaho Gov. Brad Little said in a written statement. “His sound legal judgment, deep knowledge of Idaho and unwavering commitment to doing what is right have been invaluable to our state.” Davis also served as co-chairman of the 2021 Idaho Commission for Reapportionment , which was charged with redrawing Idaho’s congressional and legislative boundaries following the 2020 census to ensure political representation is proportional. During a 2025 interview with the Idaho Capital Sun, Davis called serving as U.S. attorney, “the best job I ever had.” “… to work with these people who are genuinely trying to even-handedly apply the laws of the United States of America,” Davis said. “It impressed me then, and it impresses me now.” GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE Governor says Davis strengthened relationship between Justice Department and Idaho Idaho Gov. Brad Little gives a press conference after delivering his annual State of the State address on Jan. 6, 2025, in the Lincoln Auditorium in the Idaho Capitol. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Idaho is responsible for prosecuting federal crimes in Idaho, defends the United States in civil cases and collects debts owed to the United States, the office said. In the past year under Davis’ leadership, the office said it has filed 298 criminal charges, including 103 drug trafficking cases, 89 violent crimes cases, 69 immigration cases and 22 fraud cases. “During his time as U.S. Attorney for Idaho, Bart strengthened the relationship between Idaho and the U.S. Department of Justice and represented our state with integrity and professionalism,” Little said. “ We will miss his counsel, his wisdom and his steady leadership. I am grateful for Bart’s many years of service and friendship, and I wish him all the best as he enters retirement and has more time to enjoy with his wife, children and grandchildren.” Davis and his wife, Marion, have six children and 14 grandchildren. Davis and Marion recently celebrated their 50th wedding anniversary. YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE. SUPPORT

items.body: Independent U.S. Senate candidate Todd Achilles, left, and Independent Leadership Council co-founder Adam Brandon speak about Achilles' commitment to not caucus with either major party, to only serve two terms, hold public town halls and participate in debates if elected. Achilles held the press conference on Oct. 7, 2026, at the Idaho Statehouse in Boise. (Photo by Laura Guido/Idaho Capital Sun) Idaho independent U.S. Senate candidate Todd Achilles on Wednesday pledged to not caucus with either party if he’s elected. 2026 Voter Guide The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote. Read More Achilles, who served in the Idaho Legislature as a Democrat before announcing his independent run for U.S. Senate, is running against incumbent Republican Sen. Jim Risch , who’s in his 18th year as a senator. Achilles was joined at the Idaho state Capitol in Boise by Adam Brandon, the co-founder of a national advocacy organization promoting independent candidates called the Independent Leadership Council . Achilles also committed to serve a maximum of two terms, hold town halls in each of Idaho’s 44 counties every two years, and to engage in public debates. Brandon previously was president of FreedomWorks, which helped tea party candidates get elected to office. That organization dissolved in 2024 , Politico reported. “Every vote that he casts, both parties are going to have to come to him for his vote to represent the state of Idaho, and I think that is incredibly, incredibly powerful,” Brandon said. Idaho US Senate candidates weigh in on tariffs, Iran War, federal spending and more In the letter Achilles signed to make these commitments, he said the U.S. Senate rules would still guarantee him a committee seat despite not caucusing with the major parties. The two independent U.S. senators — Angus King of Maine and Bernie Sanders of Vermont — both caucus with Senate Democrats. When King won his election in 2012, he announced he would caucus with the Democrats because it would allow him to participate more in the committee process, PBS News reported at the time. Committee assignments are largely decided by party leaders and then formally voted on by the entire Senate. During the event, Achilles also signed a sworn, notarized statement that would resign him from office in 2039 — meaning if elected, he would only be able to serve two, six-year terms. A spokesman for the Achilles campaign said the letter will be sent to either the governor’s office or secretary of state to keep. “We’re serious about this,” Achilles said Wednesday. “That’s it. I don’t want to spend more than 12 years in D.C. I love Idaho’s mountains. I want to get back here and get my skis on and do what I love doing. So two terms. That’s it.” YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE. items.body: Hundreds of Timberline High students walked out of school Wednesday morning to call for accountability as police investigate a threat targeting another student. According to an online petition , members of Timberline’s football team used Snapchat to “call for a female student to be raped and killed.” Police began investigating the reported threats last week after Timberline officials contacted Boise police. District officials have said police asked the district to pause its own investigation to avoid interference with the case. The district has said it will conduct its own investigation once police allow it to proceed. Even if the police investigation does not result in criminal charges, district officials said the students involved could still face discipline for violating school policy. The situation has circulated on social media and prompted district leaders to cancel Timberline’s homecoming football game and postpone other related events. More than 200 students stood in protest across the street from Timberline High Wednesday morning, crowding the front of a Starbucks that closed its drive-through to accommodate them. I remain fully committed to our district and to ensuring a thoughtful transition in the months ahead.” Board Chair Lara Stone said Foudy has kept students at the heart of the district and made contributions that will benefit schools for years to come. “We are tremendously grateful for Superintendent Foudy’s leadership, commitment, and service to Blaine County School District,” Stone said in the release. The announcement gives the school board plenty of time to find a replacement. Trustees will discuss next steps at the Oct. 13 board meeting. Blaine County School District has faced several challenges this year, as EdNews reported. Trustees in January voted to cut 16.4 staff positions to save $1.7 million, but that was not enough to cover the district’s budget deficit. After years of deadlocked negotiations with the teachers’ union, trustees in September voted to impose contract terms . In one of Idaho’s wealthiest counties — with a high cost of living — Foudy is the state’s fourth-highest-paid superintendent with a salary of $198,450.

items.body: Hundreds of Idahoans gathered in the rotunda of the Idaho Capitol on Jan. 12, 2026, to protest proposed cuts to the state's Medicaid program. The protest, organized by Idaho Voices for Children, took place before the governor's State of the State Address. (Photo by Christina Lords/Idaho Capital Sun) One thing we know for absolute certain in Idaho: Our people understand the value of Medicaid expansion. We voted to adopt Medicaid expansion in 2018 through ballot initiative started after years of inaction by the state Legislature, with more than 60 percent of Idaho voters supporting expanded healthcare access. When the state Legislature became very active in attempts to weaken and repeal that voter-approved expansion seemingly as soon as they could, Idahoans showed up. They traveled to Boise to let lawmakers know that the program was not a suggestion, but a mandate and more than 80,000 of our friends, family and neighbors relied on it. Idaho’s Medicaid work requirements start in January. Here’s how they will work. Some of the busiest days at the Capitol are when everyday Idahoans show up to have their voices heard on a healthcare bill when lawmakers have tried to repeal the program or institute confusing bureaucracy via work requirements. The halls are packed and hearing rooms overflow with Medicaid supporters who vastly outnumber those who advocate cuts at around 100-1 … and the one is very often not somebody from Idaho. Most Idahoans, myself included, don’t think much about the details of our health insurance until we need it. For someone with cancer, that could mean discovering at a doctor’s appointment, while scheduling a scan, or even in the middle of treatment or recovery that they no longer have Medicaid coverage due to the work requirements that will add red tape to the program starting in January. Then what? Do they delay treatment while trying to navigate the paperwork? Do they skip a follow-up appointment or prescription they can no longer afford? For most, there isn’t another insurance option waiting in the wings. Originally, district officials had planned to postpone the homecoming football game, which had been scheduled for Thursday. However, given the heightened emotions, threats of violence, and the simple need to pause, reflect and process, we believe it is not only the prudent decision, but the right one as well.” An “additional police presence” is on site at Timberline, district officials said in a question-and-answer page on the reported threat. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) Idahoans voting in November’s general election will decide whether to give the Idaho Legislature the sole power to regulate marijuana and other drugs — and eliminate their right to bring a citizen-led ballot initiative to do so. 2026 Voter Guide Dates to know, how-to instructions and candidate surveys for Idaho’s top contested races. Read More Currently, there are two ways in Idaho that marijuana, medical cannabis or other drugs can be legalized and regulated. First, the Idaho Legislature could pass a law to legalize it. Second, Idaho voters could legalize it by passing a ballot initiative. Who gets to decide is a big part of the debate over House Joint Resolution 4, or HJR 4 for short. House Joint Resolution 4 is a proposed amendment to the Idaho Constitution that would give the Idaho Legislature the sole authority and power to legalize marijuana (including medical marijuana), narcotics and other psychoactive substances. If a simple majority of voters vote “yes” for House Joint Resolution 4, Idahoans would not be allowed to bring a ballot initiative forward to legalize marijuana, medical cannabis, narcotics or other psychoactive substances. If voters vote “no” and don’t approve HJR 4, there would be no changes to the Idaho Constitution. That means Idahoans would still be able to use the ballot initiative process to legalize marijuana, narcotics or other psychoactive substances. Voters in several of Idaho’s neighboring states, including Washington, Oregon, Montana and Nevada, used ballot initiatives to legalize marijuana in those states. People have tried to do the same in Idaho. But so far, each effort has failed to meet the signature-gathering requirements to qualify for an election, the Idaho Capital Sun previously reported. David Adler is president of the nonprofit Alturas Institute in Idaho Falls. (Photo courtesy of David Adler) Adler has taught courses on government and the Constitution at all three of Idaho’s public universities and has spoken about HJR 4 this fall. “The more I speak on it, the more I realize people generally are of the belief that this is about regulating marijuana and they don’t understand that it has a far broader impact on their ability to resort to the initiative to exercise their rights,” Adler said. “Really, HJR 4 asks Idahoans to surrender both their rights and their powers to shape their future,” Adler said. He said a ballot initiative is a tool of democracy that the public has used to improve the state since the 1930s. items.body: Joleen Noble, executive director of the Idaho Diaper Bank, says the nonprofit organization typically provides more than 75,000 diapers to children in need per month. (Photo courtesy of the Idaho Diaper Bank) As a mother of two small children (ages 2 and 5), there’s no need to lecture Jolleen Noble of Meridian about the cost of diapers – which could run close to $200 a month per child. And there’s no need to talk to her about other paycheck-eating costs such as daycare, medical emergencies and clothing. She knows all about the challenges of making ends meet. Noble, of course, can’t solve all of the financial problems. But as the executive director of the Idaho Diaper Bank , she’s providing some welcome relief in at least one area. And there are no forms to fill out, or financial statements to submit. “People who need diapers need our help,” she said. There are limits. Noble’s nonprofit organization will provide up to 50 diapers a month per baby, which doesn’t cover the entire cost for diapers. But it does make the monthly diaper tab less daunting. “Diapers are expensive, and they just add to the cost of everything else,” she said. The diaper bank gets a large portion of its supply from the National Diaper Bank Network, buying bulk from manufacturers and regional diaper drives. Mary Kay Link, an Idaho Diaper Bank board member for seven years, sees how the organization helps mothers and families. She volunteers with the Holy Apostles St. Vincent de Paul of Meridian , one of 43 working partners that distribute diapers. “SVDP has many single moms who work and need food and diapers to make ends meet. Saving money on diapers allows them to use the money to pay bills or put gas in their car,” she said. Noble has been the executive director for almost a year, and demands for the service are growing. “When the diaper bank started in 2014, they were giving out 8,000 diapers a month, and when I started it was 50,000 per month. Typically, we give out 75,000 to 100,000 per month … last month we gave 119,000.” Noble says that level of growth would not happen without her board of directors. “We have an incredible all-volunteer board that has helped shape Idaho Diaper Bank into what it is today,” she said. “I would not be in the position I am today, or able to do what I do, without the support, leadership and willingness to jump in wherever they are needed.” The diaper bank’s 43 partners also contribute to the success. Susan Rohrbacher sees the needed help through Parma Community Schools, which serves more than 25 babies per month. “This partnership has been especially meaningful for families of children with special needs,” she said. “The Idaho Diaper Bank is truly making a difference by easing financial stress and helping our families feel supported and cared for.” As with other nonprofit organizations, Noble sees challenges. “The biggest need is sustainable funding that allows us to grow our reach. Our funding comes from grants and in-kind donations. There is no government assistance,” she said. “Simply put, if we want to send more diapers out the door, we have to bring more diapers and funding in the door,” Noble said. “Space is becoming another challenge. As we think about serving more families and potentially expanding, sustainable funding and the capacity to store the product becomes increasingly important.” One big way individuals and businesses can help is through diaper drives. “Some of my favorite moments are seeing people in the community rally around a diaper drive,” she said. “Those drives bring in product and monetary donations, of course, but they also get people talking about diaper needs and introduce people to our mission. It’s pretty incredible to watch.” The Idaho Diaper Bank is living up to its slogan, “Changing Babies. Changing Lives.” GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE

items.body: The rotunda of the Idaho Statehouse as seen on Jan. 14, 2026, in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) When two mental health clinic owners in Idaho set out to restore critical services for people with severe mental illness, they faced an uphill battle. The Idaho Legislature was gearing up for across-the-board budget cuts. But Laura Scuri and Ric Boyce armed lawmakers with information and data — and spent time talking to journalists when four patients died after the mobile treatment service had been cut. Ric Boyce, director of Mental Health Specialists, testifies before the Idaho Legislature’s Medicaid Review Panel on Dec. 15, 2025 in Rexburg. (Photo by Kyle Pfannenstiel/Idaho Capital Sun) The two often worked behind the scenes, directly with lawmakers instead of testifying before committees. “We formed individual relationships with half the Legislature pretty much,” Boyce recalled in an interview. In the end, the programs that they advocated served as a rare instance of a budget cut that state lawmakers reversed. On the final day of this year’s legislative session, Idaho Gov. Brad Little signed into law a bill that temporarily restored funding for the programs that the two providers pushed for: the Assertive Community Treatment program, a mobile program for people with severe mental illness, and peer support services, which helps people navigate treatment. After four patients died, Idaho governor approves restoring cut Medicaid mental health programs Now, a mental health nonprofit plans to honor the two. This week, the National Alliance on Mental Illness of Idaho plans to award them both the Kathie Garrett Impact Award, named after a former Idaho lawmaker. In a news release, the nonprofit said the duo’s advocacy “led to the return of those programs.” The award came as a surprise. “I don’t think either one of us were thinking for a second it’s something that would be noticed,” said Boyce, a clinical social worker who owns Mental Health Specialists, a clinic in eastern Idaho’s Chubbuck. “What was important to us was that we were able to get the clients we were working with back into the program they needed so badly. And that was enough.” Scuri, who co-owns Access Behavioral Health Services in Boise, said it’s her first award. “So it’s extra special to me — especially with the environment that we’re in, and all the changes,” she said. But he said this experience tested that conception. “What I learned was that there are ways to make change happen even when it seems hopeless,” he said. But to do that, he said, requires a lot of work — and help. While he and Scuri were talking with lawmakers, he said they also found lawmakers coming to them for answers — to questions raised by community members in letters and direct outreach on all sorts of Medicaid changes, not just the cuts they were focused on. “Even individual advocacy, of sending a single letter, cumulatively had an effect. And those things were changing the minds of legislators,” Boyce said. items.body: The exterior of the Idaho Statehouse as seen on Jan. 14, 2026, in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) Two days after a grand jury indicted a former Idaho state government employee on two felony counts of misuse of public funds, a local judge dismissed the case — after a request from the prosecutor. The case marked the first criminal charges — and a rare public update — to emerge from a yearslong investigation launched by Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador that probed how the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare doled out $72 million in federal child care grants in 2021 and 2022. The official who was criminally charged, Ericka Rupp, oversaw the grant program. In the indictment, filed in Canyon County District Court last week, the grand jury charged Rupp with two felony counts of misuse of public funds and securities, for allegedly illegally authorizing, appropriating or otherwise misusing more than $300 of the government’s money. Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador speaks at the Idaho Medal of Honor ceremony held Sept. 1, 2026, at the Idaho Statehouse in Boise. (Photo courtesy of the Idaho Attorney General’s Office) Labrador’s special prosecutor, Canyon County Prosecuting Attorney Christopher Boyd, told the Idaho Capital Sun that the amount of money allegedly misused was not specified in the indictment, but that it would’ve been an issue to determine during a potential trial. Boyd said he moved to drop the indictment based on feedback from jurors. “I, however, asked of them whether they felt the case was one worth pursuing in terms of resources,” Boyd wrote in a text message. “I truly wanted their opinion on this. They had spent several full days taking testimony. The majority of jurors felt my time was better spent focusing on the many other serious crimes they worked on.” For each count, the penalties could have been up to 14 years imprisonment and up to $10,000 in fines, according to state laws cited in the indictment. Rupp’s attorney, Scott McKay, declined to comment. In a Friday order, Third District Judge Thomas W. Whitney wrote he was dismissing the case upon the state’s request. The court hasn’t released records supporting the judge’s decision to dismiss the case. Special prosecutor Christopher Boyd argues in district court that the Idaho Office of the Attorney General should not pay legal fees associated with litigation that set to block the office’s civil subpoena. (Photo by Kyle Pfannenstiel/Idaho Capital Sun) Pending permission from the court, Boyd said he hopes to release a report with more details in the coming days. Asked whether he’d pursue charges against Rupp, or other people linked to the investigation, Boyd said: “The report should conclude my investigation.” The Idaho attorney general’s office could not immediately be reached for comment. Department of Health and Welfare spokesperson Greg Stahl directed questions about the case to parties involved. “(The Department of Health and Welfare) takes seriously its responsibility to be a good steward of taxpayer dollars and remains committed to transparency, accountability, and the appropriate use of public funds,” Stahl said in a statement. (Photo by Kyle Pfannenstiel/Idaho Capital Sun) Two former Republican attorneys general in Idaho — along with dozens of former lawyers at the office — on Thursday endorsed the Democratic challenger in the race for the state’s top attorney. Lori Hickman, who’s trying to unseat Republican Attorney General Raúl Labrador, said she wishes the race was nonpartisan. The race, she said, comes down to “who’s the best attorney to be the chief legal officer for the state of Idaho.” “I’m trying to restore the tradition of sound legal advice, regardless of who the clients are or their political affiliations,” Hickman said at a news conference announcing the endorsements. “So I’m running as a Democrat because my opponent’s a Republican.” Democratic candidate for Idaho attorney general Lori Hickman stands in front of more than a dozen deputy attorneys general, and two former Republican AGs, who endorsed her in the 2026 election. (Photo by Kyle Pfannenstiel/Idaho Capital Sun) Hickman stood outside the old Ada County Courthouse across the street from the Idaho State Capitol, beside a pool of attorneys who she said collectively have hundreds of years of experience. Hickman is an Idaho attorney with two decades of experience, including at global tech company Micron, and has served as board chair of Mormon Women for Ethical Government. Labrador is a former Idaho congressman and an immigration attorney. He became the state’s attorney general in 2023, after defeating the state’s longest-serving attorney general, Lawrence Wasden, in the Republican primary election. Wasden was among the pack endorsing Hickman. At the press conference, he and former Idaho Republican Attorney General Jim Jones, who also served as a state Supreme Court justice, cheered by her side. In a Republican-controlled state, Hickman’s election bid faces tough odds. Voters in the state last elected a Democrat to statewide office in 2002, for the superintendent of public instruction. Idaho’s last Democratic attorney general was Larry Echohawk in 1995. In a statement, the Labrador campaign seemed unsurprised by the endorsements. “Lawrence Wasden, Jim Jones, and disgruntled former employees. Who would have thought?” the attorney general’s re-election campaign said. Rep. Steve Berch, D-Boise, has raised $212,580.79 as of Tuesday afternoon. Although Republicans control a supermajority in the Idaho Legislature, Berch is the only candidate in Idaho’s 105 legislative districts who has raised more than $200,000 this year. Through Idaho Sunshine, the public can search for candidates, political action committees, campaign expenditures, campaign contributions, reports and more. Berch also raised the most money heading into this year’s primary elections , the Idaho Capital Sun previously reported. In an interview Tuesday, Berch attributed his fundraising success to engaging directly with voters and knocking on tens of thousands of doors in his legislative district. “It’s really very humbling, and it tells me that people like what I’m doing in terms of knocking on doors, holding in-person town hall meetings and sending out very detailed newsletters so they know the reason why I vote the way I do,” Berch said. Most of Berch’s campaign contributions came from people and from within Idaho. According to online state campaign finance reports, Berch raised $153,816 from people, $27,450 from companies, $9,000 from political committees and $1,000 from Democratic central committees. Berch raised $169,226 in Idaho and $22,040 from out-of-state donors, records show. The rest of Berch’s campaign money was un-itemized. 2026 Voter Guide Dates to know, how-to instructions and candidate surveys for Idaho’s top contested races. Berch’s opponent in the Nov. 3 general election, Republican Steve Keyser, has reported raising $13,592.67. District 15 is one of the rare truly split legislative districts in Idaho. For the past two years, Berch held one of the legislative seats in District 15 while Republicans held the other two. Two years before, Berch and the Democrats controlled two of the district’s seats while Republicans held just one. For that reason, both Republicans and Democrats will be looking to pick up a seat in District 15 in November’s general election What other Idaho legislative candidates are raising the most money Among the 10 Idaho legislative candidates who raised the most campaign money in 2026, seven are Republicans and three are Democrats. Two candidates from the Republican primary election for Idaho Senate District 1, Sen. Jim Woodward and former Sen. Jones, although running as a Democrat, believes the position should be nonpartisan and has announced he will unaffiliated the day after the election. The treasurer’s office serves as the state’s chief financial officer — which includes overseeing the receipt of state money, accounting for disbursement of funds, investing idle state money, and administering the unclaimed property program , the 529 College Savings Fund, and the Idaho ABLE savings accounts. Each of the candidates are focused on the state’s investment strategy, but with different approaches and metrics for success. YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE. He previously ran Boise-based Harmonic Investment Advisors. He is a longtime institutional portfolio manager and a chartered financial analyst, which is an internationally recognized professional certification for advanced investment management and financial analysis, he said. “I’m a very logical individual, and I’m also a former college golfer, so I’ve spent my entire life competing, where numbers matter more than how someone dresses, what party they’re in, and so forth,” Jones said. “… You either post the score on the golf course, or you don’t. You either do well at managing investment portfolios, or you don’t.” Idaho’s 2026 election voter pamphlet is coming to a mailbox near you Ellsworth , 64, was first elected as state treasurer in 2018 after serving 12 years non-consecutively as an Idaho state representative. She has been a public school teacher, and a mediator and business consultant. She said she wants to run again because her work has helped the state. “I think I’m doing a good job, and I can see that it elevates Idahoans,” Ellsworth said. “It’s very uplifting. The main focus of my job is to assure that money is safe in the state of Idaho, that it is collected in a uniform manner. … and then when money is going to be spent but is idle at the time, we invest it. And I love turning money back to Idaho taxpayers.” How would the candidates manage Idaho investments? When the state has funds that aren’t yet ready to be spent, the treasurer’s office can invest the money to try and grow the fund until it’s ready to be spent. The Treasurer Investment Advisory Board reviews policies and performance of funds, and private firms that contract with the state help oversee investments with the treasurer. Jones said the state’s portfolios have been underperforming. He highlighted recent reports from the investment advisory board showing state funds, such as the IDLE fund , producing total returns less than a comparable index fund. An index fund tracks performance of a certain index — or group of investments that often have something in common — and tries to mimic it through buying a representative sample of stocks and bonds in that index.
